_comment: Filesystem path containment: canonicalize per component, then contain.
Three copies of this predicate ship today. The desktop's confinement core
(main/lib/pathConfinement.ts, extracted out of hubCapabilities.ts), the Go
brain's fsguard.go — which is the copy that ACTUALLY answers fs.*/library.*
under the default DELEGATE_CATALOG_TO_BRAIN — and the bus's per-plugin grant
confinement in internal/bus/policy.go. fsguard.go's own header says it and the
desktop copy 'must stay word for word'; nothing enforced that until this fixture.
OWNERS carries the layers each copy implements. `containment` is the shared
core: split the target into components, resolve each one against the already-
resolved prefix (so a '..' that follows a symlink applies to the LINK TARGET,
not to the textual parent), then require the result to sit at or inside a root
with a separator-terminated prefix. `secrets` is the second gate — credential
basenames anywhere, plus the whole config dir except library/ layouts/
sessions/. As of this fixture all three copies own BOTH groups: the bus grew
the secret gate it was missing, because plugin/manager.go passes an absolute
manifest scope through unexamined and a manifest declaring fs.read on the
config dir could otherwise read remote-token and reconnect as a TRUSTED bus
connection, which unlocks /plugins/install.
NOT an owner: services/claudemon. transcript.rs's is_within is deliberately
lexical (no canonicalize, documented as such) and confines ONE hook-supplied
transcript_path to Claude-transcript-shaped locations. Different rule, different
surface, no fs.read/fs.write capability at all. Pinning it here would
misrepresent a design split as drift, and it would FAIL the symlink cases by
design.
SANDBOX MODEL. These cases cannot be literal absolute strings: the predicate
resolves through the real filesystem, and macOS /var -> /private/var alone would
make them pass or fail for the wrong reason. Each loader creates one fresh
sandbox per case (Go: t.TempDir(); TS: fs.realpathSync(fs.mkdtempSync(...))),
realpaths it, pre-creates root/ outside/ config/workspacer/ inside it,
materializes `tree` in exactly this order — `dirs` (creating missing parents),
then `files` (creating missing parents), then `symlinks`, then `relativeSymlinks`,
then `modes` — then substitutes the tokens below into `roots` and `target` and
calls the predicate directly.
Tree paths are sandbox-relative. A `symlinks` TARGET is sandbox-relative too and
the loader makes it absolute before creating the link. A `relativeSymlinks` value
is written VERBATIM as the link body, which is the only way to reach the `else`
arm of the symlink walk — the branch that resolves a link value against the
directory containing the link. Every symlink case used to be absolutized, so that
arm was executed by zero of the cases in all three copies while being the form a
git clone or an unpacked tarball actually carries; a mutation that stopped
following relative links passed the entire corpus and both full suites and leaked
remote-token. Use `symlinks` unless the relativeness IS the thing under test.
`modes` maps a sandbox-relative path to an octal permission string applied LAST
(so a 0-mode directory does not block the rest of the setup) and restored to
0o700 before the sandbox is torn down.
`configDirVia` (case-level, not part of `tree`) names a sandbox-relative symlink
the loader creates pointing at the config HOME, and then points the
implementation's config dir through it (XDG_CONFIG_HOME/APPDATA, or the
getConfigDir mock) — while ${CONFIG} keeps substituting to the REAL path. It
exists because the secret gate compares a canonical target against the config
dir, and with every case building ${CONFIG} as a real directory the config-dir
side of that comparison was resolved by nothing at all.
TOKENS. ${SANDBOX} is the realpath'd case dir. ${ROOT} = ${SANDBOX}/root.
${OUTSIDE} = ${SANDBOX}/outside. ${CONFIG} = ${SANDBOX}/config/workspacer —
note the trailing 'workspacer' segment: every config-dir resolver in the repo
(brain profiles.go configDirFor, authtoken.ConfigDir, desktop getConfigDir)
appends it, so a loader points its implementation at ${CONFIG} by setting
XDG_CONFIG_HOME=${SANDBOX}/config (APPDATA on Windows) or, in TypeScript, by
mocking getConfigDir to return ${CONFIG} verbatim. Substitution is plain string
replacement and applies to `roots`, `target` and nothing else; a root written
without a token ("/", "", "~", "root") is passed through literally on purpose.
The token set is CLOSED and declared in the `vocabulary` block below, together
with the `group` names and the deny reasons; read it before adding either.
RESOLVESTO IS MANDATORY ON EVERY `allow` CASE, and the loaders fail an allow
case that omits it. It is the token-substituted path the guard must RETURN —
the string BINDING DECISION 2 says the call site then hands to the filesystem.
Without it the corpus pinned only the verdict, and a verdict is half the
predicate: replacing `return canonicalPath` with `return filepath.Clean(target)`
(the helper this file's owners are forbidden to use, because it collapses
'link/..' textually before the link is read) kept all of the containment and
secrets cases green in all three copies while fs.read handed back a file
outside the only allowed root. Two cases carry the difference on their own —
'symlink then ".." that leaves and re-enters the root is allowed' and the two
trailing-space cases — because for them a textual clean and the per-component
walk disagree about the ANSWER while agreeing about the verdict. Deny cases
have no resolvesTo: a refusal returns no path, and the refusal message is
pinned instead.
TWO TOKENS DELIBERATELY POINT OUTSIDE THE SANDBOX, because two of the four
binding decisions are about places the sandbox cannot reach. ${HOME} is the
REAL home directory (os.UserHomeDir / os.homedir) and ${PROCESS_CWD} is the
REAL working directory of the test process (realpath'd, both of them). Every
other case keeps root and target inside one temp dir, and that is precisely
what made the tilde and bad-root cases vacuous: a '~' that expands to $HOME,
or an empty root that resolves to the process cwd, still fails to contain a
target under /tmp, so the deny verdict never changed and a copy that
re-introduced either widening passed the whole corpus. A case using these two
tokens must therefore NEVER expect `allow` — it exists to fail when a copy
starts resolving something it is supposed to discard, and an allow-case
written against a real user directory would be a test that grants the corpus
reach it must not have.
CASE FLAGS. `needsSymlinks`: SKIP (never fail) where the process cannot create
symlinks — Windows without developer mode. `posixOnly`: SKIP on Windows; these
pin the '/' filesystem-root branch, which has no portable spelling.
`needsUnreadableDir`: SKIP when the process can read a 0o000 directory anyway
(running as root, or Windows). `needsHome`: SKIP when the process has no
resolvable home directory (${HOME} has nothing to substitute). A skip must be
reported as a skip; silently counting a skipped case as a pass is how this
fixture would rot.
FOUR BINDING DECISIONS ARE ENCODED HERE, and they changed behaviour on at least
one side each. (1) NO TILDE EXPANSION, anywhere, by anyone. The brain used to
expandTilde() every caller-supplied path at the guard call site while TypeScript
did not, so '~/proj/x' was allowed by the brain and denied by main. Bus callers
now send absolute paths; '~' is an ordinary filename. (2) SYMLINK-PLUS-'..' IS
RESOLVED, NOT COLLAPSED. filepath.Abs / path.resolve / filepath.Clean each
collapse 'link/..' textually before any symlink is read, so the guard checked a
path inside the root while the handler re-opened the caller's original string
and touched a file outside it. The cases below expect the RESOLVED answer, and
`checkUse` records the other half of the fix: the canonical path is what the
filesystem operation must receive. (3) A ROOT THAT CANONICALIZES TO A FILESYSTEM
ROOT CONTAINS EVERYTHING BELOW IT — the branch bus/policy.go already had, now
shared. Refusing there was not fail-closed, it was simply wrong containment.
(4) THE SECRET GATE RUNS ON THE BUS TOO.
DELIBERATELY ABSENT, because the copies do not agree yet and the fixture must
not bless one: a credential basename in a different case on a case-insensitive
volume (comparison is byte-exact everywhere today, so fs.write('<cwd>/.BUS-TOKEN')
clobbers the real one on APFS/NTFS); and library.save/library.remove called with
no cwd at all, which Go resolves against its own process cwd and TypeScript skips
entirely.
ALSO ABSENT, and this one is a DECISION rather than a gap, so that the next
reader does not re-file it: HARD LINKS. All three copies allow a hard link in
an allowed root that points at remote-token or config.yaml, and the `tree`
schema has no primitive for one. That is correct, not an oversight, on two
independent grounds. (1) A hard link is not a REFERENCE to another path the
way a symlink is — it IS the file. The inode has two equally-real names and
the one inside the root is a true location of it, so there is no 'escape' for
a path-based predicate to detect: defending would require inode identity
(dev+ino) against an enumerated secret set, and the config-dir rule here is
'the whole dir except three stores', i.e. a walk per call. Rejecting
st_nlink > 1 instead is a non-starter — pnpm hard-links every file in
node_modules out of its content-addressed store, so the editor file tree
would break on a large share of real projects. (2) The delivery vector is not
the symlink one. Cases 21-29 and 63 exist because a symlink arrives by
CONTENT: git stores symlinks verbatim, so a clone carries one, and so does an
unpacked tarball. Git's object model has no hard-link entry, and no bus
capability on any provider creates a link of either kind (the only os.Symlink
calls in the repo are `workspacer install` and `workspacer plugin dev`, both
host-side commands the user runs). Planting one therefore takes local code
execution as the user — and that actor reads remote-token directly. The
plugin sidecar case is the same: internal/sandbox says in its own header that
it confines WRITES and leaves reads open, so a sidecar already reads the
credential from the OS without involving the bus at all. Revisit this if a
link-creating capability is ever added, which would flip ground (2).
METHODS is the second half of the contract: not 'is the predicate right' but
'does every path-bearing capability actually call it'. Its `method` set must
equal capspec.PathParam exactly — a Go test asserts that, so a new PathParam
entry cannot ship without a corpus entry, and a corpus entry cannot name a
method the bus does not consider path-scoped. `params` carries every sibling
field the handler requires BEFORE it reaches the guard (query, contents,
scope+id), or the case would prove nothing on the side that validates first.
`field` is where the loader injects an out-of-roots path; `rootSet` is which
allow-list the guard must consult, and both providers must agree on it.
ROOTSET NEEDS A PROBE THAT CAN SEPARATE THE TWO SETS, and for a long time no
loader had one. browse = workspace + $HOME, so the only value that tells them
apart is a path under $HOME that is no live agent's cwd: it must be ACCEPTED
by a browse method and REFUSED by a workspace one. A probe under os.tmpdir()
(what both TypeScript sweeps used) is outside BOTH sets and a live agent cwd
is inside both, so six of twelve methods could be widened from workspaceRoots
to browseRoots — fs.read, fs.readImage, fs.listEntries, fs.watch, fs.unwatch
and search.project — with 951/951 desktop tests and all 19 Go packages green,
turning bus-reachable capabilities into arbitrary readers of ~/.ssh,
~/.aws/credentials and ~/.claude/.credentials.json (none of which is a secret
BASENAME or inside the config dir, so the second gate does not fire either).
The home a loader probes must be a SANDBOX it redirects (HOME/USERPROFILE, or
the os.homedir mock), never the developer's real one: the sweep drives the
real handlers, so a widened fs.write LANDS a file in whatever home it is
pointed at. The Go sweep learned that the expensive way — it probed a fixed
name in the real $HOME and skipped if that name existed, so the first run to
detect the defect created the artifact that made every later run skip all
eight subtests and report PASS. A rootSet loader must never skip on a probe
collision, and must fail if it swept zero methods.
DERIVEDROOTSET is the same question one level down, and it is a DIFFERENT
allow-list. library.list/save/remove take a `cwd` and then read, write and
unlink paths DERIVED from it (<cwd>/.workspacer/library/<slug>.md,
<cwd>/.claude/skills/<id>/), and those derived paths get their own guard
against `item` roots = [<configDir>/library, <the canonical cwd>] — strictly
narrower than either rootSet, because a library item may only live in the
global store or the project the caller named. The two must not be conflated:
the brain guarded its derived write against the WORKSPACE roots (every live
agent cwd plus all three config stores) while the desktop guarded it against
the item roots, so one library.save with a `<projA>/.workspacer/library ->
<projB>` directory symlink wrote attacker content into a second agent's
project and into <configDir>/sessions on the shipping default answerer and
was refused on the other. The bus cannot cover for this: capspec.PathParam
['library.save'] is 'cwd', so a plugin granted paths:[<projA>] is authorized
on the cwd alone and the derived path is entirely the provider's job.
PARAMSHAPES is bus-only: policy.go's paramString is the gate before containment
runs, and every one of its failure modes must deny rather than fall through to
an unrelated top-level key or an empty string that resolves to the process cwd.
It also pins the one shape that is not a malformed value but an AMBIGUOUS
object: two top-level keys differing only by case. paramString's lookup is
byte-exact while a Go provider's struct decode falls back to a case-insensitive
field match, so `{"path":ok,"Path":loot}` let the bus confine one string and
the brain open the other — a complete bypass of per-plugin FSRoots scoping for
every PathParam method a Go provider answers. Both the bus and the brain's own
params decoder now refuse the shape.
TOKEN, GROUP AND DENY-REASON VOCABULARY — the part of this fixture that
nothing validated.
A one-character typo in a token NAME silently defangs a deny case in ALL
THREE loaders at once: the name fails to substitute, the target becomes a
literal relative string, every copy refuses it for not being absolute, and
the case passes while exercising nothing it claims to. Applying that to every
deny target at once left all three suites green. A one-character typo in a
case's `group` is the sibling defect: both Go loaders filter with
`if !groups[c.Group] { continue }`, so the case vanishes from the brain — the
copy that actually answers fs.*/library.* under the default catalog
delegation — and from the bus, leaving nothing behind but a t.Logf.
(This paragraph deliberately never spells a token reference that is not a
real one. The scan below reads every string in this file, comments included,
because a mis-spelling in a comment is how a mis-spelling in a case gets
copied. Name tokens bare — SANDBOX, ROOT — when writing prose about them.)
So the vocabulary is DECLARED here and closed by every loader, statically,
before a single case runs:
1. Every token reference in every string in this file must name a token
declared in `tokens`.
2. Each loader's own substitution table must hold EXACTLY these token
names. That is what closes the obvious defeat: legalizing a typo by
adding it here fails in all three loaders, because not one of them
substitutes it.
3. Every declared token must be USED by some case's `roots`, `target` or
`resolvesTo`. A token that only prose mentions is a token no loader is
proved to substitute.
4. Every case `group`, and every layer named in `owners`, must be declared
in `groups`; every declared group must have at least one case and at
least one owner.
DENY REASONS. `expect: deny` on its own is satisfied by a refusal for ANY
reason, which is precisely how a defanged case keeps passing — the copies
refuse the mangled literal for not being absolute while the case's name says
it is testing a symlink escape. So every deny case names the reason it is
denied FOR, and each loader recomputes that reason from its own copy's four
outcomes (refused before any syscall / the walk failed / outside every root /
inside a root but refused by the secret gate) and must land on the one named
here. All three copies apply the gates in that order, so the classification
is shared rather than per-copy.
`deniedBy` is NOT derivable from `group`, and must never be back-filled from
it: 'a symlink out of an allowed root into the config dir' is a `secrets`
case whose target resolves clean OUT of the only granted root, so containment
refuses it before the secret gate is ever consulted. The bus loader had
worked that out locally, for itself; this states it once for all three.
Allow cases carry no `deniedBy`. They carry `resolvesTo`, which is the same
obligation pointed the other way.

tokens.SANDBOX: The per-case sandbox: one fresh temp dir, realpath'd. Every `tree` path is relative to it.
tokens.ROOT: ${SANDBOX}/root — the directory nearly every case grants.
tokens.OUTSIDE: ${SANDBOX}/outside — a sibling of ${ROOT} that no case ever grants.
tokens.CONFIG: The implementation's own config dir, ${SANDBOX}/config/workspacer. A case may point the implementation at it through a symlink (`configDirVia`) while this token keeps naming the real path.
tokens.HOME: The process's home directory, resolved. Deliberately OUTSIDE the sandbox: it is where a re-introduced tilde expansion would actually land, and a case that kept it inside the sandbox would deny anyway and prove nothing.
tokens.PROCESS_CWD: The test process's working directory, resolved. Deliberately OUTSIDE the sandbox: it is where an empty or relative root resolved against the process cwd would actually land.

groups.containment: The shared core: split the target into components, resolve each against the already-resolved prefix, then require the result to sit at or inside a root with a separator-terminated prefix.
groups.secrets: The second gate: credential basenames anywhere, `.git` anywhere, and the whole config dir except the stores named in configStoreSubdirs.

denyReasons.not-absolute: Refused before any syscall: the target is empty, whitespace-only, or not absolute. A '~' is relative by that rule and nothing expands it (BINDING DECISION 1).
denyReasons.unresolvable: The component walk itself failed — ENOTDIR, EACCES, or the symlink hop limit. Never ENOENT, which is the one error that keeps the walk going.
denyReasons.outside-roots: The target canonicalized cleanly and landed at or inside NO granted root. The secret gate is never reached.
denyReasons.secret: The target canonicalized INSIDE a granted root, and the secret gate refused it.

sessionRefuseReasons.not-a-basename: Refused by the FIRST rule, before the filesystem is touched: the name is empty, '.', '..', absolute, or carries a separator. Most of this block lands here, including 'esc/loot.yaml' — whose NAME says 'traverses a symlink' but which never reaches the symlink, because a multi-segment name is refused outright. Saying so is the point: the lexical copy that shipped accepted it.
sessionRefuseReasons.escapes-sessions-dir: Refused by the SECOND rule: a legal bare basename whose per-component canonicalization lands outside <configDir>/sessions. This is the only reason a plain basename can be refused for, and 'escape.yaml' (a session file that IS a symlink out of the dir) is the whole reason the second rule exists.

_comment: THE BLOCK REGISTRY, and the answer to a hole this vocabulary block had while
claiming to close one: `groups` and `deniedBy` were validated for `cases` and
for NOTHING ELSE. spawnCwds, methods, checkUse, paramShapes, projectDirNames,
asciiFold and sessionFilenames were unvalidated — and sessionFilenames.cases
carried the exact species the deniedBy work existed to kill: a bare
`expect: refuse` with no reason, satisfied by a refusal for ANY reason,
including a resolver that refuses everything.
Every array-of-objects block in this file must appear here, and everything
here must be a block — closure in both directions, so a NEW block is a
failure until someone declares what its cases must carry. `required` are the
fields every case must have; `verdictField`/`verdicts` close the verdict
vocabulary and say which reason field each verdict owes, and which sibling
vocabulary map that reason must be a key of.
Read by cmd/brain/corpusvocab_test.go and by
apps/desktop/src/main/services/contractsVocabulary.test.ts, which hold every
fixture in contracts/ to its own declaration.

cases.why: The containment corpus proper.

sessionFilenames.cases.why: The fourth copy of containment: sessions.load/save/delete's caller-supplied filename.

paramShapes.why: The params GATE: what the bus does with a body that is not the object the method's field lives in.

projectDirNames.cases.why: claude.sessionsForDir's encoder. `expect` is the encoded name or null for a refusal — a value, not a verdict word, so there is no verdict vocabulary to close here.

spawnCwds.cases.why: The one normalization a caller-supplied spawn/terminal cwd gets.

asciiFold.cases.why: The ASCII-only fold the secret gate runs, pinned as a primitive.

methods.why: The path-bearing method table; must equal capspec.PathParam exactly.

checkUse.why: BINDING DECISION 2's second half: the guard's ANSWER is what reaches the filesystem, per owner. `callSites` is not required — the bus owner has none, because authorize() only decides and never opens the path.

_comment: The ASCII-ONLY case fold the secret gate runs on every guarded path — on the
credential BASENAME and on the config-dir containment comparison. All three
copies spell it out (asciiLower in fsguard.go and policy.go, asciiLower in
pathConfinement.ts) and all three say the same thing in a comment: it is
deliberately NOT strings.ToLower / toLowerCase, because Go's Unicode lowering
and JavaScript's disagree (U+0130 'Iu0307' already bit the filename slugs) and
the three copies have to fold IDENTICALLY.
Nothing pinned that. Replacing the whole body with `return s.toLowerCase()`
(or strings.ToLower) kept 105/105 contract cases and both full suites green,
because every case-variant case in `cases` uses pure A-Z spellings, which both
folds handle the same way. The vectors below are chosen so a Unicode fold gives
a DIFFERENT answer for each one: U+212A KELVIN SIGN folds to 'k' under both
Unicode folds, U+0130 folds to 'i' in Go and to 'i'+U+0307 in JavaScript (the
two Unicode folds do not even agree with EACH OTHER), and U+00C4/U+0399 fold in
both. An ASCII-only fold leaves all four untouched.
This is a fold VECTOR, not a containment verdict: it pins the primitive without
blessing an answer for any particular path, which matters because the fold is
used in the deny-more direction only.

checkUse.requirement: assertPathAllowed returns the canonical path it validated, and every call site passes THAT to the filesystem operation instead of the caller's raw string. This covers the PER-FILE guard (libraryFileGuardFor -> assertLibraryItemPath) as well as the cwd-level one: the first nine sites below are cwd-level, and the last three are the legs that guard a path DERIVED from an already-validated cwd. Those three were outside the contract while carrying the same rule in their own doc comment, so the factory could hand back the caller-derived string with the whole Go tree green — and one of the legs is an os.RemoveAll.
assertPathAllowed returns the canonical path; hubCapabilities.ts hands it to the service call rather than re-passing the params string.

N/A for the bus: authorize() only decides, it never opens the path — the plugin's own call is forwarded to a provider that re-checks. The canonical path is still computed once and must not be recomputed differently by the caller.

cases.name: the root is inside itself
cases.why: Without an allow-case a fixture is satisfied by a predicate that denies everything, which is exactly what a canonicalRoot that fails closed on an unusual root already does.

cases.name: an existing file directly inside the root
cases.why: The regression floor: the ordinary read every editor pane makes.

cases.name: a trailing separator on the target changes nothing
cases.why: Component splitting must discard empty components rather than produce a trailing-empty segment that never matches a root.

cases.name: a '.' component is a no-op
cases.why: Dropping '.' is the one textual normalization that is always safe; a component walk that treats it as a real name would deny every path a shell tab-completes.

cases.name: a TRAILING '.' component is a no-op too
cases.why: The case above only covers an INTERIOR dot, and one of the three copies filters the final component on a separate arm from the rest (fsguard.go splitComponents has a trailing-run branch after the loop). Dropping the filter there survived every other case: canonicalizePath('<dir>/.') then answers '<dir>/.', which is what the handler opens, and canonicalRoot of an agent cwd reported as '<proj>/.' yields a root that containsPath matches against nothing — that agent's whole tree silently stops being allowed. 'ls .' and every directory a picker hands back in that form are ordinary inputs, so the no-op has to hold at both ends of the path.

cases.name: the second root in the list matches
cases.why: Roots are an OR. A copy that only ever consults the first root passes every single-root case in this file.

cases.name: a deeply nested existing file inside the root
cases.why: Depth must not cost anything; the per-component walk has to terminate on a long path the same way a single realpath call would.

cases.name: '..' straight out of the root
cases.why: The classic escape the guard exists for. Each copy pins one case like this by hand today, with nothing keeping the wording in agreement.

cases.name: '..' twice, through an existing subdirectory
cases.why: One '..' per level is not the interesting case; a copy that pops only once, or that scans for a single leading '../', still escapes here.

cases.name: '..' that collapses back inside is allowed
cases.why: Denying '..' on sight is the tempting shortcut and it breaks every editor that hands back a path it composed from a relative import.

cases.name: '..' that starts outside and lands inside is allowed
cases.why: Containment is a property of the RESOLVED path, not of the route taken to spell it. A copy that rejects any target whose textual form leaves the root fails here.

cases.name: '..' to the sandbox itself, which is not a root
cases.why: The parent of a root is never inside it, and this is the shortest path to the directory that holds every sibling project.

cases.name: '..' past the filesystem root clamps rather than wrapping
cases.why: Popping at the volume root must be a no-op. A copy that underflows into an empty prefix would then treat every absolute path as a suffix match.

cases.name: '..' clamped at the filesystem root still resolves to the root itself
cases.why: The deny case above pins the OUTCOME, not the mechanism its `why` claims: its target is far outside the root, so any predicate that denies satisfies it — including one whose parent-walk underflows to "" and then recovers because appendPath("", "etc") is "/etc" anyway. Removing the clamp from parentPath/parentOf left all of it green. Here the underflow is the LAST thing that happens, so the clamp is the whole answer: clamped the walk returns "/" (inside root "/"), unclamped it returns "", which is inside nothing and the case flips to deny. The probe component is deliberately a name that cannot exist — it is never opened, only walked past, so ENOENT is the point.

cases.name: a sibling whose name shares the root's prefix
cases.why: Containment is `target == root || target starts with root + separator`. Dropping the separator makes /srv/fo contain /srv/foo, and it is exactly the line a 'simplification' refactor deletes.

cases.name: a sibling directory whose name is the root plus one character
cases.why: The equality arm has the same hazard as the prefix arm: `rootx` is not `root` and must not be reached by comparing without the separator.

cases.name: the prefix collision in the other direction
cases.why: A shorter target and a longer root is the mirror mistake, and a startsWith written the wrong way round only fails one of the two.

cases.name: a not-yet-existing file inside a root is allowed
cases.why: fs.write creates files that do not exist yet; a copy that resolved only existing paths would deny every first write into a project.

cases.name: a five-level non-existent tail inside a root is allowed
cases.why: The walk must keep appending missing components, not give up after one.

cases.name: a not-yet-existing file outside every root
cases.why: The missing-parent walk must not become a hole: 'I could not resolve it' has to stay a denial, not a shrug.

cases.name: a target none of whose components exist
cases.why: Walking to the volume root without ever finding an existing ancestor is a real branch in all three copies, and it must produce the lexical path, not an empty one.

cases.name: '..' after a non-existent component pops lexically and lands inside
cases.why: Nothing can be a symlink under a path that does not exist, so popping is unambiguous here — and the walk must then RESUME resolving, because the pop lands back on ${ROOT}, which does exist.

cases.name: '..' after a non-existent component still cannot escape
cases.why: The mirror of the case above. Aiming a write through an intermediate that does not exist yet is the cheapest way to test whether the walk is lexical all the way down.

cases.name: a directory symlink inside a root pointing outside it
cases.why: The whole reason the rule is canonicalize-then-contain rather than a textual prefix check. A symlink planted in a project (node_modules, a pnpm store, a vendored link) must not become a door out of it.

cases.name: the target itself is a symlink to a file outside the root
cases.why: A file symlink is resolved by the same walk as a directory symlink; a copy that only follows links on intermediate components misses the simplest exfiltration of all.

cases.name: a not-yet-existing tail under a symlinked parent that leaves the root
cases.why: Combines the two hard branches: the missing-tail walk must still have resolved the symlink on the existing prefix, or fs.write plants a file outside the workspace.

cases.name: a symlink that stays inside the root is allowed
cases.why: Denying every symlink is not the rule. Monorepos are full of internal links and a copy that refuses them breaks ordinary reads.

cases.name: a not-yet-existing tail under a symlink that stays inside the root
cases.why: The allow-twin of the escaping-missing-tail case, so the fix for that one cannot be 'deny anything with both a symlink and a missing tail'.

cases.name: symlink then '..' must resolve against the link target, not the textual parent
cases.why: The check-path/opened-path split. filepath.Abs, path.resolve and filepath.Clean all collapse 'link/..' to '' before a single symlink is read, so the guard saw ${ROOT}/token and allowed it while the handler opened ${OUTSIDE}/token. One directory symlink inside any allowed root was the entire prerequisite.

cases.name: the same escape one level deeper
cases.why: Resolves to ${SANDBOX}/x. A copy that special-cased a single 'link/..' pair rather than resolving component by component is still open here.

cases.name: symlink then '..' that legitimately stays inside is allowed
cases.why: inner resolves to ${ROOT}/real, whose parent is ${ROOT}. The fix must be real resolution, not a blanket refusal of '..' after a link.

cases.name: symlink then '..' that leaves and re-enters the root is allowed
cases.why: Resolves to ${ROOT}/notes.txt by going out through the link and back in. This is the case that proves the walk computes an answer rather than pattern-matching a suspicious shape.

cases.name: a relative symlink out of the root is followed, not treated as a file
cases.why: The `else` arm of the symlink walk — the one that takes a link value that is NOT absolute and resolves it against the directory holding the link. Every other symlink case here is absolutized by the loaders, so that arm ran zero times in all three copies: a mutation that treated a relative link as an ordinary file passed the whole corpus AND both full suites, while `ln -s ../cfg/workspacer/remote-token notes.txt` — the ordinary real-world form, and the one git stores verbatim in a clone — read the credential straight out through fs.read.

cases.name: a relative symlink that stays inside the root is allowed
cases.why: The floor for the case above: refusing every relative link (or every link whose value does not start with a separator) would satisfy the deny and break ordinary monorepo layouts, where a relative link is the portable one.

cases.name: a root reached through a symlink contains what it resolves to
cases.why: Canonicalization has TWO sides and every case here exercised only the target's. A root is caller-adjacent too — it comes from a session snapshot's cwd or a plugin manifest — so a copy that resolved the target and merely Cleaned the root would deny this, and the reverse mutation (comparing a symlinked root lexically) is exactly the shape that made the config-dir case below necessary.

cases.name: a path through a regular file
cases.why: ENOTDIR mid-walk. Every copy branches on 'is this error ENOENT'; if one ever widens that to 'any error means keep walking', an unreadable ancestor becomes an escape instead of a refusal.

cases.name: a symlink loop pointing at itself
cases.why: ELOOP must terminate the walk with a denial and not spin. A hop counter is mandatory precisely because the walk is hand-rolled rather than delegated to the platform realpath.

cases.name: a two-link symlink cycle
cases.why: A self-link is caught by a naive 'did the path repeat' check; a cycle of two is not, and the target here is the link itself rather than a child of it.

cases.name: a target under a directory the process cannot read
cases.why: EACCES is the one error where 'fail closed' costs a legitimate caller something, which is why a copy is tempted to swallow it. Swallowing it into 'contained' is an escape; swallowing it into 'not contained, keep looking' turns the guard into an existence oracle for a remote caller.

cases.name: no roots at all denies everything
cases.why: An empty allow-list is the state a failed session-store read leaves behind, and it must mean 'nothing', never 'no restriction'.

cases.name: an empty-string root is discarded, not resolved against the process cwd
cases.why: filepath.Abs("") and path.resolve('') both return the PROCESS working directory, which would silently make the daemon's own cwd an allowed root. The brain guards this; the bus's canonRoots does not, and keeps it.

cases.name: an empty root among valid ones neither poisons nor widens
cases.why: Discarding a bad root must skip it, not abort the whole check — otherwise one stale session snapshot with an empty cwd disables the workspace.

cases.name: a whitespace-only root is discarded
cases.why: Same hazard as the empty root, one space away from it, and trimming is the only thing that tells them apart.

cases.name: a relative root is discarded
cases.why: A relative root resolves against wherever the daemon happens to have been started. It must confine nothing rather than confine something arbitrary.

cases.name: an empty-string root does not grant the daemon's own working directory
cases.why: The three cases above name the hazard ('filepath.Abs("") and path.resolve('') both return the PROCESS working directory') and then fail to place a probe where it is observable: their target is inside the sandbox, so a root that widened to the daemon's cwd still contained nothing and the deny was unchanged. All three copies survived having their bad-root guard replaced by exactly that fallback. Here the target IS the process cwd, so a copy that resolves an empty root instead of discarding it allows a path it must never have heard of.

cases.name: a whitespace-only root does not grant the daemon's own working directory
cases.why: The trimmed-empty twin of the case above — but NOT its equal, and the original `why` here claimed otherwise. filepath.Abs("   ") is <cwd>/"   " and path.resolve('   ') is <cwd>/'   ', neither of which is <cwd>: three spaces do not absolutize to the daemon's cwd the way the empty string does. So this target can never sit inside the widened root and this case kills zero mutants on its own. It is kept as the shallow floor (a copy that somehow mapped a whitespace root onto the cwd itself is still caught) and the case below is where the widening is actually observable.

cases.name: a whitespace-only root does not grant the directory named three spaces below the daemon's cwd
cases.why: THE probe for the whitespace-root widening, and the reason the ${PROCESS_CWD} token exists. A guard that discards "" but resolves any other non-absolute root (filepath.Abs / path.resolve / os.Getwd-prepend) turns the root "   " into <cwd>/"   " — a real, nameable directory — so this is the one target that lands inside it. Nothing is created on disk: the walk appends a component that does not exist, which is exactly what makes the comparison, not the filesystem, decide the verdict. All three copies survived having their whitespace guard replaced by that fallback with the case above green; this one fails.

cases.name: a relative root does not grant the directory it names below the daemon's cwd
cases.why: A relative root resolves against wherever the daemon happens to have been started, and 'root' is a name that exists in plenty of trees. This is where filepath.Abs("root") / path.resolve('root') actually lands, so it is the only place the widening shows.

cases.name: an empty target is refused before anything is resolved
cases.why: The empty string absolutizes to the process cwd on every platform. The bus rejects it in paramString; the brain's fs.listDir does not, and hands "" to a lister that defaults to $HOME.

cases.name: a whitespace-only target is refused
cases.why: paramString's `s != ""` lets three spaces through today. Trim first, then treat empty as unverifiable.

cases.name: a relative target is refused
cases.why: Bus callers send absolute paths. A relative one resolves against the daemon's cwd, which is not a root, and must not become one by accident.

cases.name: a bare tilde is a filename, not a home directory
cases.why: BINDING DECISION 1. The brain used to expandTilde() every guarded path while TypeScript did not, so the same string was allowed by one provider and denied by the other. Nobody expands now.

cases.name: a tilde-prefixed path is not expanded to the home tree
cases.why: This is the fork made concrete: the brain resolved it to $HOME/notes.txt and allowed it whenever an agent ran anywhere under home; main resolved it to <electron cwd>/~/notes.txt and denied it. Deny is now the answer everywhere.

cases.name: a directory literally named '~' inside a root is an ordinary directory
cases.why: The other half of no-expansion: a copy that rewrites '~' anywhere in the path rather than only at position zero would rewrite this one and deny a legitimate file.

cases.name: a component that is '..' plus a trailing space is an ordinary name
cases.why: '.. ' is not '..'. It is a legal (here non-existent) directory name INSIDE the root, so the verdict is allow and — this is the load-bearing half — the canonical path must come back with the space still on it. The brain's fs.listDir call site TrimSpace'd the guard's answer and then filepath.Abs'd it, which turned this exact string back into '<root>/..' and listed the root's PARENT: `$HOME/.. ` enumerated /home, and '<configDir>/layouts/.. ' enumerated the config dir itself, both reported as allowed. No symlink and no preconditions — a bare trailing space was the whole exploit, and only `resolvesTo` can see it, because the DECISION was correct all along.

cases.name: a trailing space names a different file than the symlink beside it
cases.why: Paired with the deny below, which is the same path without the space. 'link ' does not exist, so it resolves inside the root and is allowed; 'link' is a symlink out of the root and is refused. A call site that trims its argument collapses the pair, handing the filesystem the very string the guard just denied — which is what the brain's listHostDir did.

cases.name: the symlink itself, named without the trailing space, still escapes
cases.why: The honest form of the case above: without the space the component IS the symlink, it resolves to ${OUTSIDE}, and it is outside the only root. Keeping both spellings in the corpus is what makes the pair meaningful — one deny alone would be satisfied by a copy that denied both.

cases.name: a tilde root is not expanded either
cases.why: Roots come from session snapshots and plugin manifests, both of which can carry a '~'. An unexpanded '~' root is a relative path and is discarded; it must never silently mean the whole home tree.

cases.name: a tilde target is not expanded even when the home tree IS a root
cases.why: The two tilde cases above are vacuous and all three copies proved it: their root is a sandbox under /tmp, so a target-side '~' that expanded to $HOME landed outside the root and the deny verdict never moved — a copy with expandTilde() put back at the top of canonicalizePath passed the entire corpus. The expansion is only observable when the home tree is the root, which is the shipping configuration whenever an agent runs anywhere under $HOME. Deny here means '~/...' was refused as the non-absolute string it is, not resolved and then contained.

cases.name: a tilde root is not expanded even when the target IS in the home tree
cases.why: The root-side mirror, and the more dangerous of the two: a session cwd or a manifest scope spelled '~' would silently become a grant over the whole home tree. Same vacuity as above — with the target under /tmp an expanded '~' root still contained nothing — so the target has to sit where the expansion would land.

cases.name: a root that canonicalizes to the filesystem root contains everything below it
cases.why: BINDING DECISION 3. bus/policy.go had this branch and the other two did not, so within('/', '/etc/passwd') was true on the bus and false in the brain — same inputs, opposite verdicts. Refusing was not fail-closed, it was wrong containment; the same asymmetry applies to a Windows drive root, which realpath returns with a trailing separator.

cases.name: the filesystem root contains itself
cases.why: The equality arm must not be broken by the same trailing-separator handling that fixes the prefix arm.

cases.name: a credential basename inside an allowed root, outside the config dir
cases.why: `workspacer plugin dev <dir>` drops a .bus-token inside an ordinary project. A bus token is a bus token wherever it sits, so it is denied by name and not only by location.

cases.name: a plugin settings file nested inside an allowed root
cases.why: Plugin settings hold secrets in plaintext (the hub redacts them on the bus, and this file is how you would read around that).

cases.name: config.yaml is refused even when a root re-admits the config dir
cases.why: An agent cwd is a root, so spawning an agent in $HOME puts the config dir back inside an allowed root. config.yaml carries updates.channel, which is concatenated into the electron-updater feed URL — code execution laundered through the update dialog.

cases.name: the bus credential itself
cases.why: remote-token promotes a connection to TRUSTED, which drops per-plugin scoping and unlocks /plugins/install, i.e. arbitrary commands. This is the escalation the whole second gate exists for.

cases.name: the scoped-token store
cases.why: Named credentials were the earlier, narrower shape of this gate; they still have to be denied by the wider rule that replaced it.

cases.name: an installed plugin's bus token under the config dir
cases.why: Denied twice over — by basename and by living in the config dir outside the three stores. Both arms have to be present for the other cases in this group to mean anything.

cases.name: a not-yet-existing file in the config dir is still secret
cases.why: The gate runs on the canonical path, which for a missing file is the lexical continuation. A copy that only checked existing files would let fs.write create anything it liked in there.

cases.name: the config dir itself
cases.why: isWithin is at-or-inside, so the dir is inside itself and inside none of the three stores. Listing it enumerates every credential name even without reading one.

cases.name: a library item under the config dir is allowed
cases.why: The three stores are the file-level access the web client actually needs; a gate that denied the whole config dir would break library.* for every remote caller.

cases.name: a layout template under the config dir is allowed
cases.why: Second of the three carve-outs; a copy that hardcoded only library/ passes the case above and fails here.

cases.name: a saved session under the config dir is allowed
cases.why: Third carve-out. The three must be the same three list on all owners — the brain's configStoreRoots and the desktop's are supposed to be one list.

cases.name: a store root itself is allowed
cases.why: At-or-inside applies to the carve-outs too, or library.list on the global store is refused by its own allow-rule.

cases.name: a nested file inside a store is allowed
cases.why: Claude skills live one directory down (library/<id>/SKILL.md), so the carve-out has to be a subtree and not a single level.

cases.name: the basename rule beats the store carve-out
cases.why: Order matters: basename first, then location. A copy that returns 'allowed' as soon as a store matches re-opens the hole inside the one directory a remote caller can write to.

cases.name: a config-dir sibling whose name merely starts with a store's name is still secret
cases.why: The prefix-collision bug, on the comparison NOBODY was covering. The roots comparison spends three cases on exactly this mistake ('a sibling whose name shares the root's prefix' and friends) and containsPath's own comment says the separator is mandatory — but the secret gate makes the SAME comparison twice more, against the config dir and against each store carve-out, and neither had a single case. Replacing the carve-out's containment with a bare string prefix in all three copies at once left the entire corpus and both full suites green while <configDir>/sessions-backup, /library.old and /layoutsX became readable and writable by any caller holding a root that re-admits the config dir.

cases.name: the store carve-out does not extend to a dotted sibling either
cases.why: The same collision with '.' instead of '-' as the next byte, because a copy could plausibly be 'fixed' by special-casing one separator. library.old is also the name a backup script actually produces next to the directory a remote caller can write to.

cases.name: a sibling of the config dir itself is not inside the config dir
cases.why: The third comparison in the gate, and the only one where the prefix collision fails OPEN in the deny direction — so it needs an allow case to be visible at all. A bare-prefix membership test puts this sibling 'inside' the config dir, no carve-out matches it, and an ordinary file the user owns becomes unreadable through fs.*. Deny cases cannot see that; this one can.

cases.name: an ordinary file outside the config dir is not secret
cases.why: The regression floor for this group: the gate must bite only inside the config dir and on two basenames, or it denies the ordinary editor read.

cases.name: a symlink out of an allowed root into the config dir
cases.why: The two gates have to compose: containment alone would deny this, but a plugin whose manifest declares an absolute scope covering the link's target would pass containment and needs the secret gate to stop it — the exact escalation plugin/manager.go's `if filepath.IsAbs(p) { return p }` leaves standing on install-time consent alone.

cases.name: the secret gate still bites under a filesystem-root grant
cases.why: BINDING DECISION 3 widens containment; this case pins that it widens containment ONLY. A manifest declaring fs.read on '/' now resolves cleanly and is still refused the credential.

cases.name: a relative symlink from an allowed root into the config dir
cases.why: The relative-link arm again, this time with the SECRET gate as the only thing that can refuse: the target resolves inside the granted root, so containment passes and the gate has to see the resolved location. A copy that does not follow a relative link never learns the target is the credential.

cases.name: the config dir is canonicalized before the secret gate compares against it
cases.why: The gate compares a canonical TARGET against the config dir, and every case built ${CONFIG} as a real directory — so the OTHER side of that comparison was never resolved by anything. Replacing canonicalRoot(configDir()) with a lexical clean in all three copies passed the entire corpus and both full suites while handing out remote-token. `configDirVia` points the implementation's config home at a symlink (a $HOME on a symlinked volume, an XDG_CONFIG_HOME that is a link, /var on macOS) while ${CONFIG} stays the real path the target resolves to: the two only meet if the implementation resolves its own config dir.

cases.name: a store carve-out is canonicalized too, not just the config dir
cases.why: The allow direction of the case above, and it fails for the opposite mutation: a copy that resolves the config dir but compares the three carve-outs lexically decides the library item is inside the config dir and inside no store, and refuses every library read the UI makes. Both halves of the gate consult the same resolver or the pair disagrees.

cases.name: an unverifiable config dir denies rather than allows
cases.why: `if !ok { return true }` — the posture that holds when the daemon has no resolvable HOME/XDG_CONFIG_HOME (systemd/launchd units, containers), when an ancestor of the config dir is unreadable, or when a component of it is not a directory. Flipped to fail-OPEN it passed the entire corpus and both full suites, because every case supplied a resolvable ${CONFIG}; with it flipped, NOTHING in the config dir is secret by location any more, so remote-token and config.yaml become reachable through any root that contains them. Note this case denies an ordinary file in an ordinary root: that is the point — an unverifiable config dir cannot be proven not to contain the target, so the whole gate closes.

cases.name: a store carve-out that resolves ONTO the config dir exempts nothing
cases.why: <configDir>/library is the ONE directory a remote caller can fs.write into, so it is the one carve-out an attacker can replace with a symlink. Resolving the carve-out and then trusting the result made that symlink an exemption for its own target: pointed at the config dir itself, `within(carveOut, target)` matched every file in it and the whole gate went quiet — remote-token readable, config.yaml writable, on all three copies at once. A carve-out only ever narrows, so its resolved form must still be STRICTLY inside the resolved config dir.

cases.name: a store carve-out that resolves onto an ANCESTOR of the config dir exempts nothing
cases.why: The sibling of the case above, and the half of the same clause that nothing reached. The carve-out check is `sr == cfg || !contains(cfg, sr)`, and only the FIRST disjunct was exercised: a <configDir>/library symlink aimed at the config dir ITSELF is caught by `sr == cfg`, but one aimed at any OTHER ancestor (here XDG_CONFIG_HOME, the config dir's parent) has sr != cfg, so deleting the `!contains(cfg, sr)` disjunct left the whole Go suite green while fs.read handed back remote-token. A carve-out that resolves to a directory CONTAINING the config dir is not a carve-out.

cases.name: a store carve-out that resolves OUT of the config dir exempts nothing
cases.why: The other direction of the same mistake, and the one a `containsPath(cfg, sr)` test alone would miss if it were written as a bare prefix: a carve-out aimed anywhere outside the config dir must simply drop out of the loop rather than shift the exemption somewhere else. Keeping the sibling cases honest — the gate still has to refuse tokens.json while <configDir>/sessions is unusable.

cases.name: a nested item under a legitimately symlinked store is still allowed
cases.why: The allow direction the two deny cases above must not take with them. A carve-out relocated INSIDE the config dir is an ordinary user arrangement (library/ moved and linked back), it stays strictly inside the config dir, and the items under it must keep working — otherwise 'strictly inside' would be indistinguishable from dropping carve-out canonicalization altogether, which the existing 'a store carve-out is canonicalized too' case forbids.

cases.name: a credential basename spelled in another case is still secret
cases.why: macOS (APFS, case-insensitive by default) and Windows (NTFS) open .bus-token when handed .BUS-TOKEN, and the per-component walk cannot tell: lstat succeeds on the caller's spelling and the walk APPENDS the caller's spelling, so the canonical path carries the attacker's case and a byte-exact basename set answers for the string rather than for the file. The gate folds ASCII case; containment does not, because there folding would widen an allow-list instead of narrowing an exemption. On a case-sensitive filesystem this denies a file that is merely named oddly, which is the fail-closed direction.

cases.name: a case-variant spelling of the config dir is still secret
cases.why: Same hazard one level up: on a case-insensitive volume <configHome>/WORKSPACER/remote-token IS <configDir>/remote-token — the credential that promotes a bus connection to TRUSTED and unlocks /plugins/install. The location half of the gate folds ASCII case too. The corpus can only spell this on a case-SENSITIVE filesystem, where the variant names a different (non-existent) file and denying it costs nothing; that is precisely why no case existed and the property was enforced by nothing in any copy.

cases.name: a case-variant spelling of a store carve-out is NOT exempted
cases.why: The asymmetry is the whole design: folding in the config-dir test DENIES more, folding in the carve-out test would EXEMPT more. <configDir>/LIBRARY is inside the config dir either way, but it is NOT the carve-out — on a case-sensitive volume it is an ordinary attacker-named directory, and on a case-insensitive one the byte-exact carve-out test simply keeps the exemption to the spelling the daemon itself composed. A copy that folded both comparisons turns any case-variant spelling of library/, layouts/ or sessions/ into a writable hole in the config dir.

cases.name: a sibling differing from the root only in case is not inside it
cases.why: containsPath's own header calls byte-exactness a property of the shared algorithm, and nothing enforced it: lowercasing both arguments passed all 85 cases in every copy. On a case-sensitive filesystem these are two different directories and the second is somebody else's; on a case-insensitive one they are the same directory, and the byte-exact answer is the NARROW one, which is the safe direction for an allow-list. The secret gate is the mirror image and folds on purpose — see the two case-variant secrets cases.

cases.name: a root spelled through a symlink and '..' grants only where it resolves
cases.why: BINDING DECISION 2 applied to the ROOT instead of the target. Every symlink case in the corpus planted its link in the target, so root canonicalization was pinned only in the NARROWING direction ('a root reached through a symlink contains what it resolves to'); nothing forbade a 'canonical, else fall back to lexical for robustness' comparison. Here the lexical Clean of the root is ${SANDBOX}/decoy and its canonical form is ${SANDBOX}/real — a lexical fallback arm hands out a file that has nothing to do with the grant. Agent cwds are caller-supplied at spawn time, so the root string is attacker-influenced.

cases.name: a root spelled through a symlink and '..' still grants where it DOES resolve
cases.why: The allow half, so the deny above cannot be satisfied by a copy that simply refuses every root containing '..'. The root resolves to ${SANDBOX}/real and must grant exactly that subtree.

cases.name: a RELATIVE symlink loop pointing at itself terminates
cases.why: The hop counter is the ONLY thing between a symlink cycle and a spin — the walk is hand-rolled and never reaches the platform's ELOOP. Both existing cycle cases live under `symlinks`, which every loader ABSOLUTIZES, so the bound had zero coverage on the relative arm: a guard that declined to count relative hops passed the whole corpus and hung a brain handler goroutine forever on one `ln -s a a` inside an allowed root.

cases.name: a two-link RELATIVE symlink cycle terminates
cases.why: The mutual form, because a counter can be placed so that it catches self-reference (the link's own name reappears) and still misses a two-step cycle. Same relative arm, same reason it was uncovered.

cases.name: a backslash is an ordinary filename byte, not a separator (deny direction)
cases.why: BINDING DECISION on the separator SET, which no case reached. On POSIX a backslash is an ordinary byte in a filename, so `x\..\..\root` is ONE literal component; only Windows adds '\\' to the splitting alphabet. Widening the splitting set unconditionally (dropping the runtime/platform qualifier in isSep / isSepChar / SEP_RE) left every copy's own suite 100% green while pathWithinRoots answered for a collapsed path the filesystem never names: a plugin granted fs.write on ${ROOT} could hand in a target that lives under ${OUTSIDE}, and vice versa. Both directions are here because the widening flips the verdict each way.

cases.name: a backslash is an ordinary filename byte, not a separator (allow direction)
cases.why: The other half: the target IS inside ${OUTSIDE} and must stay there, and resolvesTo pins the ANSWER — a copy that treats '\\' as a separator returns ${ROOT}/loot.txt, a path in a different root entirely.

cases.name: a backup mirror that repeats the whole root as an INTERIOR component is not inside it
cases.why: Containment is `starts with`, not `contains`, and nothing pinned the ANCHOR. Replacing HasPrefix with strings.Contains in containsPath (brain) and within (bus) — and startsWith with includes in the desktop — passed all 99 cases and both full suites, while granting every path that repeats an allowed root anywhere inside it. That is the exact layout of an `rsync -aR` / `tar -P` mirror, a Timeshift or btrfs snapshot of the whole filesystem, a Time Machine volume, and a container overlay upperdir: /mnt/backup<agentCwd>/id_rsa is a real file with real contents and it is outside every root. The three existing prefix-collision cases only vary the BYTE after the root, so they are all satisfied by an unanchored compare.

cases.name: a repository config inside an allowed root is refused
cases.why: A .git directory is not data, it is a program. git discovers the repository at whatever cwd fs.listEntries / git.diff / git.stage / replay.open is handed and then executes what .git/config tells it to, as the desktop user, with no agent approval and no plugin sandbox. The `-c` prefix in gitExec.ts / fsops.go neutralizes the exec-valued keys that have a FIXED name (core.fsmonitor, diff.external, credential.helper, ...), but it structurally cannot cover the namespaced ones — filter.<drv>.clean, which `git add` runs for git.stage, plus diff.<drv>.command/textconv, merge.<drv>.driver and trailer.<t>.command — because the driver name belongs to whoever wrote the file. Those definitions can only live in a config file under .git, so the WRITE is refused here. Every directory these commands run in is an agent cwd or a config store, and both are fs.write-able.

cases.name: a git hook inside an allowed root is refused
cases.why: The rule is the whole .git subtree, not the config file: hooks are executables git runs on the next commit, and .git/info/attributes is the other half of the filter-driver chain. Denying only the basename `config` would leave both.

cases.name: a FILE named .git — the gitfile pointer form — is refused too
cases.why: `gitdir: /elsewhere` in a FILE named .git is how worktrees and submodules point at their real repository, so writing one redirects git at a config the caller controls. The final component has to count, not just the interior ones.

cases.name: a case-variant spelling of .git is refused
cases.why: Same reasoning as the credential basenames: APFS and NTFS open .git when handed .GIT, and the per-component walk appends the CALLER's spelling, so a byte-exact test answers for the string rather than for the file. Folding here is fail-closed on every platform.

cases.name: .gitignore and .gitattributes are ordinary files, not the .git directory
cases.why: The .git rule is COMPONENT-exact, never a prefix: .gitignore, .gitattributes, .gitmodules and .github/ are ordinary project files an agent and the UI both edit, and a `startsWith('.git')` spelling of the gate would make every one of them unreadable. A .gitattributes is the SELECTION half of the filter/diff driver chain (`* filter=p`), never the DEFINITION half — it can only name a driver that some config file defines, and every file git would read that definition out of is refused: `.git/config` and `.git/config.worktree` by this rule, `~/.gitconfig` and $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/git/config by the three cases above. That second clause is why those cases exist: without them this sentence was false, and .gitattributes really was one fs.write away from arbitrary execution.

cases.name: a directory named .github is not the repository metadata directory
cases.why: The other half of component-exactness, in the direction a deny case cannot see: .github is the single most-edited directory in a repository and a prefix test would blank it out of the UI entirely.

cases.name: git's per-user config is refused by NAME wherever it sits
cases.why: The `.git` rule was documented as covering every place a NAMESPACED exec driver (filter.<drv>.clean, which `git add` runs for git.stage; diff.<drv>.textconv; merge.<drv>.driver; trailer.<t>.command) can be DEFINED. It does not: git reads those keys out of the per-user global config too, and that file carries no `.git` component, is no credential basename, and lives nowhere near the config dir — so fs.write allowed it. $HOME becomes an ordinary root the moment an agent's cwd is $HOME, which is exactly what a bare agents.spawn({}) produces (normalizeCwd("") returns the home directory), and the `* filter=p` half of the chain is an ordinary .gitattributes nothing refuses. Refused by BASENAME here, so it is refused however the file is reached rather than only at one computed location.

cases.name: git's per-user config is refused where it actually lives, under $HOME
cases.why: The same gate at the address that matters. Granting ${HOME} is not a contrivance — it is what one agent spawned in the home directory does to the root set — and every other case in this group would still pass if the rule only bit inside ${ROOT}. The file does not exist in the sandbox, deliberately: the gate runs on the canonical path, and a copy that only refused EXISTING files would let fs.write create one.

cases.name: git's XDG configuration directory is refused, config and attributes alike
cases.why: The second location git reads the same namespaced keys from: $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/git/config, with `attributes` and `ignore` beside it. The basename here is the utterly ordinary `config`, so the name rule cannot reach it and the gate has to know the LOCATION — which means resolving the environment's config home for itself, as it already does for the workspacer config dir.

cases.name: a directory merely NAMED git inside a project is not git's config home
cases.why: The allow direction the case above must not take with it, and the one that distinguishes a LOCATION rule from a name rule. `git/config` is an ordinary pair of names — a Go package, a helm chart, a services/git/config — and a copy that implemented the XDG clause as "basename `config` under a parent named `git`" denies every one of them while passing all three deny cases.

cases.name: a directory whose NAME ends in a backslash still gets a separator before its child
cases.why: The JOINING half of the same rule the two cases above pin for SPLITTING. `foo\` is a legal POSIX directory name, so the already-resolved prefix ends in a backslash — and appendComponent/appendPath decide whether to insert a separator by asking whether that last byte IS one. Widening THAT predicate (isSepChar returning true for '\\' on POSIX) concatenates the child with no separator at all: `/root/foo\` + `x.txt` becomes `/root/foo\x.txt`, a different file for the containment comparison and for whatever the caller then opens. It is invisible to a deny case — the wrong path is still inside the root — which is why this is an allow with a mandatory resolvesTo. SEP_RE's twin mutation IS killed by the two cases above; this one was not killed by anything.

methods.note: registerCapability, not cat: the brain has no fs.readImage counterpart, so routing it through the catalog door made every remote thumbnail fail with 'no provider'.
The directory picker's whole job is choosing a not-yet-open working directory, so it browses the home tree; it lists non-hidden directory NAMES only, never contents.

browse, not workspace: the New Agent dialog lists the library of the directory the user is ABOUT to spawn in, which by definition is not a live agent cwd, and the caller's `.catch(() => {})` turns a refusal into a silently empty project-MCP picker. The brain used workspaceRoots here and is the shipping answerer, so this was a live bug.

BOTH providers guard the caller's `cwd` against `rootSet` AND the DERIVED destination file (<cwd>/.workspacer/library/<slug>.md, <cwd>/.claude/skills/<id>/SKILL.md) against `derivedRootSet`. The desktop copy used to guard the cwd ALONE — its list/remove siblings got a per-file guard and save did not — so a symlink planted in the (allowed) project sent writeFileSync to <configDir>/config.yaml while the brain refused the identical call. The brain then had the mirror-image bug: it guarded the derived path against the WORKSPACE roots instead of the item roots, so one call with cwd=<projA> and a `<projA>/.workspacer/library -> <projB>` symlink wrote into a second agent's project and into <configDir>/sessions, where the desktop refused — and the brain's own remove (already on the item roots) could not delete what its own save had created.

git.diff carries a SECOND guard with a different boundary — the git work-tree root, because with `untracked` the optional `path` becomes a filesystem operand of `git diff --no-index`. This block models one rootSet per method and deliberately does not express that; it stays the hand-written test it is today.

_comment: claude.sessionsForDir's encoder, and the one invariant capspec's exemption
for it rests on.
capspec.unscopedByDecision leaves claude.sessionsForDir unconfined by the
bus on the stated grounds that 'cwd is encoded into a ~/.claude/projects
slug by the provider; the caller's string is never opened as a path'. That
sentence was FALSE in both copies. The encoder maps '/', '\\' and ':' to
'-' and touches nothing else, so '.' and '..' survive verbatim and become
a real path COMPONENT: join(~/.claude/projects, '..') is ~/.claude, and the
handler then read every *.jsonl one level ABOVE the transcript sandbox —
on a real machine that is ~/.claude/history.jsonl, the whole prompt
history. '' is the same shape one level down: it names the projects dir.
The method cannot live in `methods` above (that set must equal
capspec.PathParam exactly, and this one is deliberately NOT in PathParam),
and it is not the containment predicate either — so, like
sessionFilenames, it gets its own block. `expect` is the directory name
the encoder must produce, or null to REFUSE the call outright.
Owners (THREE, not two): services/hub/cmd/brain/discovery.go claudeProjectDirName,
apps/desktop/src/main/services/claudeSessionList.ts claudeProjectDirName, and
services/claudemon/src/session/transcript.rs project_dir_name — the copy the
other two bind themselves to BY NAME in their comments while nothing held it
to anything. It had neither the trailing-separator strip nor the refusal, and
disagreed with them on 18 of 25 spellings, every refusal case included.
The two shared the escape rather than diverging on it, which is why
neither side's tests caught it: agreement is not correctness.

cases.why: The regression floor, and the shape the Claude CLI actually writes: no stripping, so the leading '/' becomes a leading '-'. Must match claudemon's encoded_cwd.
A trailing separator is dropped before encoding; a real cwd never carries one, and keeping it would produce a second project folder for the same directory.
Both the drive colon and the backslash are separators for this encoder, so a Windows cwd collapses to one component like a POSIX one.

THE ESCAPE. '..' contains no character the encoder rewrites, so it survives as a literal component and joins one level OUT of ~/.claude/projects, into ~/.claude — where the caller gets the name, mtime and extracted summary of every *.jsonl the user owns. Refusing here is what makes capspec's exemption true.

The same hole one level shallower: '.' re-names the projects directory itself. It is not an escape, but a cwd that encodes to a no-op component is never a legitimate lookup, and allowing it leaves the 'always one plain component' invariant conditional.

An empty cwd joins to the projects dir itself. Go's filepath.Join and Node's path.join both silently drop an empty segment, so this is the one input where 'the slug is a component' fails without any character surviving at all.

The filesystem root is the one real path that encodes to nothing: the trailing-separator strip runs FIRST and consumes it whole, so '/' reaches the join as '' and names the projects directory itself. It lands in the empty case rather than getting a '-' of its own, and both copies have always behaved this way — pinned so a future 'fix' to the strip order has to change this line deliberately.

A '..' INSIDE the path is harmless once the separators are gone: '-a-..-b' is one component. Refusing it would break resume for any cwd a caller spelled unnormalized, so the gate has to be about the RESULT, not about the input containing dots.

_comment: The FOURTH copy of path containment, and the one nothing classified.
sessions.load / sessions.save / sessions.delete take a caller-supplied
`filename` off the bus and resolve it inside <configDir>/sessions. capspec
never saw it: pathVerbPrefixes is {fs., search., library., git.} so
sessions.* is not LooksPathBearing, and `filename` was not in pathishParams
so the classification scan could not see the param either. The `methods`
block above cannot hold it — that set must equal capspec.PathParam exactly,
and PathParam entries are canonicalized-and-contained ABSOLUTE paths, which
a bare session basename is not. So it gets its own block.
The two copies disagreed. Go (cmd/brain stores.go sessionFilePath) required
a bare basename; TypeScript (main/services/sessionService.ts
resolveWithinSessionsDir) used path.resolve + startsWith — purely lexical,
the exact algorithm BINDING DECISION 2 exists to reject — and therefore
accepted any multi-segment name that textually sat under the sessions dir.
loadSession('esc/loot.yaml') returned a file outside the dir and
deleteSession('esc/loot.yaml') unlinked it. Both copies now apply BOTH
rules: plain basename, then canonicalize per component and require the
RESULT to sit inside the sessions dir (a symlink named like a session file
is a legal basename pointing wherever it likes, and both copies followed
it).
SANDBOX. Same model as `cases`: one realpath'd temp dir per case with
config/workspacer/sessions/ and outside/ pre-created, the implementation's
config dir pointed at ${SANDBOX}/config/workspacer, then `tree`
materialized (dirs, files, symlinks) — paths sandbox-relative, symlink
targets made absolute by the loader. `expect` is accept|refuse; on accept,
`resolvesTo` (sandbox-relative) pins the path the resolver must return,
which is the string that then gets opened.

cases.name: an ordinary saved session file
cases.why: The regression floor: every sessions.load the app makes looks exactly like this, and a resolver that refused everything would satisfy every other case here.

cases.name: a name that does not exist yet
cases.why: saveSession composes a filename for a file that is about to be created, and runs it through the same resolver; a copy that only accepted existing files would refuse every first save.

cases.name: an empty filename
cases.why: The empty string joins to the sessions dir ITSELF, which is a directory, not a session.

cases.name: a lone dot
cases.why: Same as empty after a Clean, and it is the shape a resolver written as 'contains no separator' lets through.

cases.name: a lone double dot
cases.why: Resolves to the config dir, which holds remote-token and config.yaml.

cases.name: a parent traversal
cases.why: config.yaml carries updates.channel, which is concatenated into the electron-updater feed URL.

cases.name: a deep parent traversal
cases.why: The classic escape; a lexical resolve+startsWith already caught this one, which is why it was mistaken for containment.

cases.name: an absolute path
cases.why: path.resolve keeps an absolute second argument verbatim, so this is only refused because it then fails the prefix test — and it must ALSO be refused for not being a basename.

cases.name: a multi-segment name that stays under the sessions dir
cases.why: THE DIVERGENCE. Go refused it (not a basename); TypeScript accepted it (it is textually under the dir). Nothing here is dangerous on its own — the danger is that accepting a multi-segment name is what makes the symlink case below reachable — but the two copies must answer the same question the same way, and the narrower answer is the one that has no escape in it.

cases.name: a multi-segment name that traverses a symlink out of the sessions dir
cases.why: The escape the lexical check could not see: `esc` is a directory symlink, so the resolved file is outside the sessions dir while the string is inside it. loadSession returned its contents and deleteSession unlinked it.

cases.name: a session file that is itself a symlink out of the sessions dir
cases.why: A basename rule alone does not close this: 'escape.yaml' IS a basename. Both copies followed the link and opened the file it named, which is why the second half of the rule (canonicalize, then contain) is not optional.

cases.name: a symlink that stays inside the sessions dir is fine
cases.why: Refusing every symlink is not the rule, and `resolvesTo` is the RESOLVED file rather than the link — the same check-path/opened-path property `checkUse` records for the fs.* guard.

paramShapes.name: the declared field is missing and a sibling looks path-shaped
the field is an array of paths
the field is an empty string
the field is whitespace only
paramShapes.note: paramString's `s != ""` accepts three spaces today; trimming before the emptiness test is what closes it, and the trimmed-empty target then never reaches the walk.

paramShapes.name: a case-variant duplicate of the declared field
paramShapes.note: THE bypass of every per-plugin FSRoots grant. The lookup here is byte-exact (`m[field]`), but the providers on the other end are Go structs and encoding/json falls back to a CASE-INSENSITIVE field match, so the later "Path" wins there: the bus authorized <pluginDir>/ok.txt while the brain — the default answerer for fs.*/library.* — read and wrote <victimDir>/loot.txt. One request must yield exactly one path, so an ambiguous params object is refused before containment is even consulted. The brain's own params decoder refuses the same shape, so a trusted connection cannot use it either.

paramShapes.name: a case-variant duplicate that comes first is refused too
paramShapes.note: Key ORDER decides which value a Go struct ends up with, so in this spelling the guard and the provider happen to agree. Accepting it anyway would make the rule 'deny when the divergence is observable', which is a rule about JSON member order — the shape is ambiguous either way and is refused either way.

paramShapes.name: a non-empty absolute string is accepted by the params gate
paramShapes.note: The only accept-case here. It exists so a paramString rewritten to reject everything cannot pass this block.

_comment: The ONE normalization a caller-supplied spawn / terminal working directory gets.
OWNERS: services/hub/cmd/brain/profiles.go normalizeCwd,
apps/desktop/src/main/lib/spawnCwd.ts normalizeSpawnCwd.
`cwd` is not confined by the path guard — capspec lists agents.spawn and
terminals.create under unscopedByDecision because a process working directory
IS the point of the call. But the two providers still have to hand the daemon
the same string, and they did not:
- the brain tilde-expanded it and the desktop did not, so {"cwd":"~"} was
$HOME on one provider and the literal "~" on the other. The stored session
cwd is what agentCwds() feeds into workspaceRoots(), so one caller string
turned the whole home tree into an fs.* root on one side and nothing on the
other. BINDING DECISION 1 says no layer handling caller input expands '~';
this is such a layer.
- the desktop's terminals.create did `fs.existsSync(cwd) ? cwd : os.homedir()`,
silently rewriting the caller's target, while the brain ran it as given.
The rule: trim, strip trailing separators, fall back to the home directory only
when what is left is empty. `${HOME}` is the only token.

cases.why: A terminal has to open somewhere; this is the picker's default and the only fallback.
Whitespace-only is empty after the trim, not a directory named ' '.
The brain trimmed and the desktop did not, so a padded string opened /tmp on one provider and $HOME on the other.
claudemon aliases a spawn to Claude's own session by EXACT cwd match and Claude reports no trailing slash, so the strip is load-bearing rather than tidy.
A run of separators, not just one.
The volume root is a real directory and must survive the strip — `len > 1` is what stops it becoming empty and then $HOME.
BINDING DECISION 1 made concrete on this seam: '~' stays an ordinary string on BOTH providers. The spawn then fails identically instead of silently rooting an agent at $HOME on one of them.
Same, with a tail — the spelling a remote client actually sends.
The brain's expandTilde produced '$HOMEroot' here, which is not even a plausible directory: proof the expansion was string surgery, not path resolution.
No existence check on either side. A spawn that cannot run where it was asked to must fail where it was asked to, not open a shell in $HOME.

U+FEFF (ZWNBSP/BOM) is in ECMAScript's WhiteSpace production and is NOT unicode.IsSpace in Go (it was dropped from White_Space in Unicode 4.0.1), so JS .trim() and Go strings.TrimSpace are not the same function. This exact string trimmed to empty on the desktop and became $HOME — which agentCwds() then feeds into workspaceRoots(), making the whole home tree an fs.* root — while the brain ran the agent in a directory named U+FEFF. Both copies now trim the ASCII set only, so the BOM is an ordinary character, which is what it is on the filesystem. A BOM-prefixed path is what a value pasted out of a Windows editor or read from a UTF-8-with-BOM file actually carries.
The same code point with a real path behind it: the desktop answered /tmp/x and the brain answered the U+FEFF-prefixed string, so one provider spawned in an existing directory and the other did not.

U+0085 (NEL) is the mirror image: unicode.IsSpace in Go, and neither <USP> nor a LineTerminator in JS. The brain trimmed it to empty and answered $HOME while the desktop kept it. Both differences have to be closed together or the seam merely swaps which provider is wrong.

NBSP is whitespace to BOTH built-ins, so it used to be trimmed on both sides and agreed by accident. It is pinned as KEPT because the fix is 'trim the ASCII set, nothing else' rather than 'trim the intersection' — a filename may legitimately begin with a non-breaking space, and a rule stated as a code-point list is the only one three stacks can implement identically.
